Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
or ionic: Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s)

State symbols not required for the mark.

At A the rate at which heat is given out by the reaction equals the rate at which heat is lost to the surroundings, so the temperature stops rising.

“The reaction has finished” does not score.

Extrapolate the cooling line back to the time the zinc was added (2 min), not to the y-axis: about 26.7 °C.

ΔT ≈ 26.7 − 17.0 = 9.7 °C (9.6–9.8 accepted).

Why: this corrects for heat lost while the reaction was happening.

q = mcΔT = 50.0 g × 4.18 J g−1 °C−1 × 9.7 °C = 2027 J = 2030 J (3 s.f. required; ECF from (d)).

Assume the solution has the density and specific heat capacity of water.

Use the limiting reagent: 0.0100 mol Cu2+.

ΔH = −2030 J ÷ 0.0100 mol = −203 000 J mol−1 = −203 kJ mol−1 (negative because exothermic).

Any two:

  • heat lost to the surroundings (polystyrene beaker is not a perfect insulator);
  • solution assumed to have the specific heat capacity of 50 g of water;
  • heat absorbed by the metals (Cu and excess Zn), beaker and thermometer ignored;
  • not carried out under standard conditions.

Energy/enthalpy (y-axis) against reaction coordinate (x-axis):

  • Products line drawn below reactants (exothermic).
  • ΔH = vertical gap from reactants to products.
  • Ea = gap from reactants up to the top of the uncatalysed hump.
  • Ecat = smaller gap from reactants to a lower hump.
  • Axes or reactant/product levels labelled.

Drawing it endothermic caps the mark at 4.

(i) ΔT = 44.6 − 23.2 = 21.4 °C; mass of solution = 100 + 10 = 110 g.

q = mcΔT = 110 × 4.20 × 21.4 = 9887 J ≈ 9.89 kJ (using 100 g loses a mark).

(ii) n(NaOH) = 10.0/40.0 = 0.250 mol; ΔH = −9.887 kJ / 0.250 mol = −39.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative because the solution warmed).

(iii) Heat is lost to the surroundings (beaker, air), so the temperature rise and |ΔH| are too small. Improvement: use an insulated polystyrene cup with a lid (or account for the heat absorbed by the glass).

(i) + means energy is absorbed (endothermic, e.g. bond breaking); − means energy is released (exothermic, e.g. bond making). Both needed for the mark.

(ii) ⦵ means standard conditions: 298 K (25 °C) and 100 kPa (1 atm in older papers), substances in their standard states.

Any two assumptions: all the heat released goes into the solution (no heat lost to the surroundings); the cup and the zinc absorb negligible heat; the solution has the density (1.00 g cm−3) and specific heat capacity (4.18 J g−1 K−1) of water; the temperature is uniform throughout the solution.

Why: the expression uses the volume of solution as its mass and the c of water, so it ignores everything else that could take up heat.

(i) Extrapolate the cooling line back to when the zinc was added (t = 100 s): T = −0.050(100) + 78.0 = 73.0 °C. Initial temperature = 24.8 °C, so ΔT = 73.0 − 24.8 = 48.2 °C (accept 47–49). Using the highest temperature recorded would underestimate ΔT; extrapolating corrects for heat lost while the reaction ran.

(ii) q = mcΔT = 50.0 g × 4.18 J g−1 K−1 × 48.2 K = 10 074 J ≈ 10.1 kJ.
ΔH = −q / n = −10.1 kJ ÷ 0.0500 mol = −201 kJ mol−1 (accept −197 to −206). The negative sign is needed: the temperature rose, so the reaction is exothermic.

(i) The more negative the standard electrode potential of Mn+/M, the more negative (more exothermic) the enthalpy change when M is added to CuSO4(aq). Do not just say “greater enthalpy change”; the direction must be clear.

(ii) Sketch any line (straight or curved) with a positive gradient that crosses ΔH = 0 at about the E° of copper (between +0.25 and +0.50 V). Metals above copper (e.g. Ag) give no reaction, so the line may flatten at 0 there.

Why: the further apart the two E° values, the more strongly the metal reduces Cu2+, and the more energy is released.

(i) Mass burned = 80.557 − 80.034 = 0.523 g; n = 0.523 ÷ 32.05 = 0.0163 mol.

(ii) ΔT = 26.4 − 21.5 = 4.9 K; q = mcΔT = 20.000 × 4.18 × 4.9 = 410 J = 0.41 kJ.

(iii) ΔHc = −q ÷ n = −0.41 ÷ 0.0163 = −25 kJ mol−1. The negative sign is essential: combustion is exothermic. +25 scores only 1 mark.

(i) The value in (a) is for water formed as a gas. The data-booklet value is for standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa), where water is a liquid. The difference is the enthalpy of vaporization of water.

(ii) Much of the heat is lost to the surroundings (air, test tube, stand) instead of going into the water, and combustion may be incomplete. Just writing “heat lost” is not enough; say where the heat goes.

(i) n = 3.99 ÷ 159.61 = 0.0250 mol.

(ii) Extrapolate the cooling line back to the time of mixing (120 s): maximum ≈ 26.1 °C. Starting temperature = 19.1 °C, so ΔT = 7.0 °C (accept 6.9–7.1).

(iii) q = mcΔT = 50.0 × 4.18 × 7.0 = 1463 J ≈ 1.5 kJ. Using 53.99 g gives 1.6 kJ, which is also accepted.

(iv) ΔH1 = −1.5 ÷ 0.0250 = −60 kJ mol−1 (accept −58 to −60). The value must be negative because the temperature rose.

(i) % error = |78.0 − 67.6| ÷ 78.0 × 100 = 13.3% (10.3% if 70.0 is used).

(ii) The “anhydrous” solid had already absorbed some water from the air, so it was partly hydrated. Less heat is released when it dissolves, so ΔH1, and therefore ΔHx, comes out less exothermic (less negative) than the true value.

(i) y-axis labelled enthalpy (not energy); reactants (NaOH + HNO3) level drawn above products (NaNO3 + H2O); downward arrow labelled ΔH = −57.6 kJ mol−1.

(ii) The products are more stable: they are at lower enthalpy (energy is released; exothermic).

(iii) n(NaOH) = 0.0500 × 2.50 = 0.125 mol; heat change = 0.125 × (−57.6) = −7.20 kJ (7.20 kJ released).

q = mcΔT = 100.0 × 4.18 × 3.50 = 1463 J (1.46 kJ)
n(NH4Cl) = 5.35/53.5 = 0.100 mol
Temperature fell, so endothermic: ΔH = +1.46/0.100 = +14.6 kJ mol−1 (using 105.35 g gives +15.4, also accepted).

(i) q = mcΔT = 50.0 g × 4.18 J g−1 K−1 × 21.3 K = 4450 J = 4.45 kJ.
n(CH3OH) = 0.230 / 32.05 = 7.18 × 10−3 mol.
ΔHc = −4.45 / 7.18 × 10−3 = −620 kJ mol−1 (−6.20 × 102).
The answer needs a negative sign and units. Use the mass of the water, not the methanol, in q.

(ii) The experimental value is less exothermic than the Data Booklet value (−726 kJ mol−1), so less heat was transferred to the water. This is probably due to heat loss to the surroundings or incomplete combustion. Improvement: insulate or shield the calorimeter and flame, account for the calorimeter's heat capacity, or extrapolate a temperature–time graph to correct for heat loss.

(i) M(MgSO4) = 24.31 + 32.06 + 4(16.00) = 120.37 g mol−1; n = 3.01/120.37 = 0.0250 mol.

(ii) ΔT = 26.7 − 17.0 = 9.7 K. q = mcΔT = 50.0 × 4.18 × 9.7 = 2027 J = 2.03 kJ (mass of water, density 1.00 g cm−3).
ΔH1 = −2.03/0.0250 = −81 kJ mol−1 (2 s.f., since ΔT has 2 s.f.). Negative because the temperature rose (exothermic). Using the total mass 53.01 g gives −86 kJ mol−1, also accepted.

Any two of:

  • heat lost to the surroundings;
  • the MgSO4 was not completely anhydrous (had absorbed water) or was impure;
  • specific heat capacity/density of the solution assumed equal to pure water;
  • not all the solid dissolved;
  • the mass of the 7H2O was ignored in the calculation;
  • literature values are measured under standard conditions, the experiment was not.

(i) The heat (enthalpy) change when molar amounts of reactants react as in the equation, under standard conditions (100 kPa, 298 K).

(ii) n = 1.00 × 0.0500 = 0.0500 mol; energy = 0.0500 × 57.9 = 2.90 kJ.

(iii) n(NaOH) = 2.50/40.00 = 0.0625 mol; q = mcΔT = 50.0 × 4.18 × 13.3 = 2780 J = 2.78 kJ; ΔH = −2.78/0.0625 = −44.5 kJ mol−1 (negative: temperature rose).

(iv) Hess's law: NaOH(s) → NaOH(aq) (−44.5) then neutralization (−57.9): ΔH = −44.5 + (−57.9) = −102.4 kJ mol−1.
Heat loss to the surroundings. Not all of the energy released reaches the water, so the measured |ΔHc| is too low.

(i) ΔT = 30.2 − 25.0 = 5.2 °C (K). If heat loss is allowed for by extrapolating, +5.6 is also accepted.

(ii) q = mcΔT = (25.0 + 27.0) g × 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 5.2 K = 1130 J = 1.13 kJ.
n = 0.0250 mol.
ΔH = −1.13 ÷ 0.0250 = −45 kJ mol⁻¹. It is negative because the reaction is exothermic; +45 scores 2 of 3.

(iii) % error = |(−45) − (−58)| ÷ 58 × 100 = 22% (2 s.f.).

(iv) Heat loss to the surroundings. Improve by using better insulation, for example a polystyrene cup with a lid. 'Use a calorimeter' alone is not enough.
Extrapolate the rising (temperature-increase) section of the graph back to 0 cm3 of acid. The line meets the axis at about 21.4 °C (21.2–21.6 °C accepted).

Extrapolate the rising line and the cooling line until they cross – the crossing point is the maximum temperature corrected for heat loss.

HCl: ≈ 30.4 °C
CH3COOH: ≈ 29.0 °C

(i) Total volume = 50.0 + 26.0 = 76.0 cm3, so m = 76.0 g. ΔT = 29.0 − 21.4 = 7.6 K.
q = mcΔT = 0.0760 kg × 4.18 kJ kg−1 K−1 × 7.6 K = 2.4 kJ. Using only 50 cm3 for the mass is a common error.

(ii) n(NaOH) = 0.995 × 0.0500 = 0.04975 mol (= moles of water formed).
ΔH = −2.4 kJ ÷ 0.04975 mol = −48 kJ mol−1 (−48 to −49). The negative sign is needed: the reaction is exothermic.

Ethanoic acid is a weak acid – only partially ionized.

Some of the energy released is used to ionize the remaining CH3COOH molecules (an endothermic step) before they react with OH−, so less heat is released overall than with fully ionized HCl.

(i) q = mcΔT = 80.0 g × 4.18 J g−1 K−1 × 7.5 K = 2.5 × 103 J = 2.5 kJ. CuSO4 is limiting (0.0160 mol), so ΔH = −2.5 kJ ÷ 0.0160 mol = −1.6 × 102 kJ (−1.8 × 102 kJ also accepted using 0.0137 mol Cu formed). Negative because the temperature rose (exothermic).

(ii) Any one: density of the solution is 1.00 g cm−3; its specific heat capacity equals that of water (4.18 J g−1 K−1); the reaction goes to completion; no side reactions. (Not “no heat loss” – already stated.)

(iii) % uncertainty in ΔT = 0.2 ÷ 7.5 × 100 ≈ 3 %. This carries through to ΔH: 0.03 × 160 kJ ≈ ±5 kJ.
